query: For a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy used as a thin coating on a conventional metal substrate, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation during sliding in the intended high-temperature operating regime? Define a controlled change relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the corresponding directional changes in wear and deformation, state the regime in which those predictions should hold, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Under high-temperature sliding, the wear resistance and microscopic deformation of the FeNiCrCoCu HEA coating are primarily governed by the formation of a dynamically recrystallized, ultra‐nanocrystalline near-surface layer that promotes deformation twinning over dislocation pile-up. A controlled post‐deposition thermal treatment that refines the near-surface grain size will lead to lower wear rates and a deformation microstructure characterized by increased twin density relative to the as-deposited (coarser-grained) baseline.
generation.material_initial_state: FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy thin coating on a conventional metal substrate in its as-deposited condition with a relatively coarse near-surface microstructure.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled post-deposition thermal treatment (annealing) designed to induce near-surface grain refinement and promote dynamic recrystallization.
generation.conditions: High-temperature sliding regime (e.g., temperatures above 600 °C) under conditions of reciprocating or continuous sliding contact.
generation.structural_mediator: An ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer featuring a high density of deformation twins and refined grains.
generation.mechanism: During high-temperature sliding, shear stresses and local heating trigger dynamic recrystallization at the surface. The refined grains and increased twin boundaries accommodate strain more effectively, reducing dislocation accumulation and delaying crack initiation, thus enhancing wear resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline coating, the thermally pre-treated (annealed) coating will exhibit a reduced wear rate, a smoother worn surface, and microstructural evidence (via TEM/SEM) of a finer nanocrystalline layer with enhanced twin formation, while dislocation pile-up regions are reduced.
generation.baseline: The as-deposited coating with a coarser near-surface grain structure.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to be effective under high-temperature sliding conditions (above ~600 °C) where dynamic recrystallization and twin formation are active; uncertainties remain at temperatures where rapid oxidation or additional environmental processes may dominate.
generation.uncertainty: The precise degree of grain refinement needed, the role of possible concurrent oxidation, and the balance between twin- and dislocation-mediated plasticity require further quantification. Also, the relative contribution of stress-induced versus thermally activated processes is not fully isolated.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeNiCrCoCu HEA coatings on identical metal substrates. One set remains in the as-deposited state (baseline) and the other undergoes a controlled post-deposition annealing treatment designed to refine the near-surface grains. Subject both sets to high-temperature sliding wear tests under identical load, speed, and temperature conditions (e.g., >600 °C). Then, use microscopic analysis (TEM/SEM) to characterize the surface microstructures and quantify twin densities and dislocation arrangements, while also measuring wear rates and friction coefficients.
measurements: Grain size distribution and twin density (via TEM/SEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed (grain-refined) coating does not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in wear rate and does not show increased twin formation (or equivalently, shows no clear difference in deformation mode) compared to the baseline as-deposited coating under the same high-temperature sliding conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Combining Machine Learning and Molecular Dynamics to Predict Mechanical Properties and Microstructural Evolution of FeNiCrCoCu High-Entropy Alloys

Abstract: AbstractCompared with traditional alloys, high-entropy alloys have better mechanical properties and corrosion resistance. However, their mechanical properties and microstructural evolution behavior are unclear due to their complex composition. Machine learning has powerful data processing and analysis capabilities, that provides technical advantages for in-depth study of the mechanical properties of high-entropy alloys. Thus, we combined machine learning and molecular dynamics to predict the mechanical properties of FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloys. The optimal multiple linear regression machine learning algorithm predicts that the optimal composition is Fe33Ni32Cr11Co11Cu13 high-entropy alloy, with a tensile strength of 28.25 GPa. Remarkable Wear Resistance in a Complex Concentrated Alloy with Nanohierarchical Architecture and Composition Undulation

Abstract: AbstractSustained wear damages on the sliding surfaces of alloys are generally the culprit responsible for the failure of various mechanical systems. Inspired by high-entropy effects, here we deliberately deploy nanohierarchical architecture with composition undulation in a Ni50(AlNbTiV)50 complex concentrated alloy, which yields ultralow wear rate within the order of 10−7 to 10−6 mm3/Nm between room temperature and 800 °C. Such remarkable wear resistance heretofore represents one of the highest wear resistance reported for the bulk alloys or composites, and originates from the multi-type adaptive friction interface protection governed by intrinsically nano-coupled grains and nanoprecipitates. This cooperative heterostructure releases gradient frictional stress in stages upon wear at room temperature through the coexistence of multiple deformation pathways while activating a dense nanocrystalline glaze layer upon wear at 800 °C to minimize adhesive and oxidative wear. Evidence of Inverse Hall-Petch Behavior and Low Friction and Wear in High Entropy Alloys

Abstract: AbstractWe present evidence of inverse Hall-Petch behavior for a single-phase high entropy alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) in ultra-high vacuum and show that it is associated with low friction coefficients (~0.3). Grain size measurements by STEM validate a recently proposed dynamic amorphization model that accurately predicts grain size-dependent shear strength in the inverse Hall-Petch regime. Wear rates in the initially soft (coarse grained) material were shown to be remarkably low (~10–6 mm3/N-m), the lowest for any HEA tested in an inert environment where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide films is mitigated. The combined high wear resistance and low friction are linked to the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer. The dynamic amorphization model was also used to predict an average high angle grain boundary energy (0.87 J/m2).
